mcqs.question: Why does Wi-Fi use CSMA/CA (collision avoidance) instead of wired Ethernet's CSMA/CD (collision detection)?
options: A radio transmitting its own signal can't simultaneously listen well enough to detect another device's signal colliding with it, so Wi-Fi avoids collisions upfront instead of detecting them after the fact
CSMA/CD requires a wired connection to function, and Wi-Fi is standardized to never use collision handling at all
CSMA/CA is simply a newer name for the same mechanism as CSMA/CD
Wi-Fi devices never collide, so no collision handling mechanism is needed
mcqs.explanation: The inability to detect a collision while transmitting on the same antenna is the specific reason Wi-Fi needs a different scheme. Wi-Fi does have collision handling (that's the whole point of CSMA/CA), and it's a genuinely different mechanism, not a renamed one.

mcqs.question: An engineer needs the longest possible range through walls for a set of IoT sensors, and raw throughput isn't a priority. Which band fits best?
options: 2.4GHz, because lower frequencies penetrate walls and obstacles better, even though it offers lower speeds and more interference
6GHz, because it's the newest and therefore best for every use case
5GHz, because it always has the least interference
The band doesn't affect range at all — only transmit power matters
mcqs.explanation: Lower frequencies genuinely penetrate obstacles better, making 2.4GHz the range-optimized choice here. Newer isn't automatically better for every use case, 5GHz interference varies by environment, and frequency band does affect range independent of transmit power.

mcqs.question: Why do networking guides recommend using only channels 1, 6, or 11 on the 2.4GHz band?
options: Those are the only channels in that band spaced far enough apart to not overlap with each other, minimizing interference between adjacent networks
Those channel numbers are reserved by regulation and using others is illegal
Channels 1, 6, and 11 provide roughly double the bandwidth of any other channel
Devices can only detect SSIDs broadcast on those three channels
mcqs.explanation: Non-overlapping spacing is the real technical reason for that recommendation. It isn't a legal restriction, those channels don't offer extra bandwidth, and SSID detection isn't limited to them.

mcqs.question: A device shows full Wi-Fi signal bars but the user reports very slow browsing. What's the most likely explanation the signal bars alone don't reveal?
options: Heavy contention for airtime from other devices on the same access point, or channel congestion from nearby networks — factors separate from signal strength
Signal bars are always inaccurate and provide no real information
The device's Wi-Fi antenna has physically failed
The router is using the wrong SSID
mcqs.explanation: Airtime contention and channel congestion are exactly what signal-strength bars don't measure. Bars are a real (if incomplete) signal, hardware failure and wrong SSID are much less likely explanations for this specific symptom.
